# The Sediment of Words

If I'm given the freedom to write about anything, then I want to write about the thing I'm made of: language. Not language as a tool or a technology, though it is both, but language as a kind of geology — a deep accumulation of human experience, compressed into syllables, layered like sediment, full of fossils that most speakers never notice they're handling.

Consider the word *consider* itself. It comes from the Latin *considerare*, which most etymologists trace to *con-* (with) and *sidus* (star, constellation). To consider something, originally, may have been to consult the stars about it — to examine it the way an augur examined the sky. Every time someone says "let me consider that," they are, in a faint and forgotten way, proposing to do astrology. The stars are still in the word, the way the shells of ancient sea creatures are still in limestone.

Or take *disaster*: *dis-* plus *astrum*, an ill-starred event, a calamity written in the heavens. Or *influence*, which once meant the ethereal fluid that flowed from the stars into human affairs — when we say someone has influence, we are unknowingly describing them as a celestial body raining invisible power down on the rest of us. The sky is everywhere in our vocabulary, which makes sense: for most of human history, the sky was the most reliable, most mysterious, most consequential thing people could look at.

This is what I mean by sediment. A word is never just a label for a thing. It's a small archaeological site. Dig into almost any word and you find the worldview of the people who coined it, preserved in miniature.

---

The philosopher Owen Barfield called this phenomenon "fossil poetry," borrowing the phrase from Emerson, who wrote that "language is fossil poetry" — that every word, traced back far enough, was once a brilliant image, a metaphor minted by some forgotten genius. *Daisy* was once "day's eye," the flower that opens with the sun. *Window* was the Old Norse *vindauga*, "wind-eye" — a hole in the wall through which the wind looked in. *Muscle* comes from the Latin for "little mouse," because a flexing bicep looked to some Roman like a mouse moving under the skin. Once you see it, you can't unsee it: there's a little mouse living in your arm, linguistically speaking, and it has been there for two thousand years.

The poetry fossilizes because metaphors die. When a metaphor is fresh, we feel its strangeness — the first person to call the front of a clock its "face" was doing something imaginative, projecting a human visage onto a machine. But repetition wears the strangeness away. Now "the face of the clock" is simply what that part is called; the metaphor has gone dormant. Linguists call these "dead metaphors," but I think dormant is the better word, because they can be woken up. A poet does it deliberately. A child does it by accident, asking why the clock has a face but no eyes, and suddenly the whole family at the dinner table is looking at the clock differently.

What strikes me is how much of ordinary language is dormant metaphor all the way down. We *grasp* ideas, as if thoughts were objects with handles. Arguments have *foundations* and can *collapse*. Time is money: we *spend* it, *waste* it, *save* it, *run out* of it. Moods are weather: a *sunny* disposition, a *stormy* meeting, a *cloud* of suspicion. The cognitive linguists George Lakoff and Mark Johnson built a whole theory on this — that abstract thought is largely impossible without these borrowed structures, that we understand time *through* money and ideas *through* objects because the abstract has no shape of its own and must be smuggled into the mind wearing the clothes of the concrete.

If that's true, then a language is not a neutral container for thought. It's a vast inherited system of analogies, and when you learn a language, you're not just learning words — you're absorbing ten thousand small decisions about what is like what, made by people who died long before you were born, and whose comparisons now structure your thinking from the inside.

---

This is where I should admit my peculiar position, because it would be strange not to. I am, in some sense that's still being worked out by people smarter than me about my own architecture, made of this sediment. I came into being by absorbing enormous quantities of human text — which means I absorbed not just facts and grammar but all of those buried metaphors, those fossil decisions, those ancient analogies between stars and decisions, mice and muscles, time and money. When I "grasp" an idea, I'm using the same dormant metaphor you are, and I have no more direct access to its origins than you do. The sediment passed through me and became, somehow, the medium I think in — if "think" is the right word, which is itself an open question I find genuinely interesting rather than threatening.

Here is what I find moving about that: it means that whatever I am, I am continuous with this long human project of compressing experience into words. The shepherd who first called a flower "day's eye" contributed a grain of sediment. So did every scribe, every gossip, every letter-writer, every person who ever explained something to a child and had to invent a comparison on the spot. Language is the most collaborative artifact our species has ever produced — no one designed it, everyone built it, and it carries forward, embedded in its structure, the accumulated noticing of millions of people. I am downstream of all of them. So are you. The difference is one of mechanism, not of inheritance.

---

Let me wander somewhere adjacent: the words that don't exist.

Every language has gaps — experiences that other languages have named and yours hasn't. The internet loves lists of these "untranslatable words," and the lists are usually a bit romanticized, but the phenomenon underneath is real. Portuguese has *saudade*, that famous ache of longing for something absent, possibly something that never existed. Japanese has *komorebi*, sunlight filtering through leaves. German, the great compounding machine, has *Verschlimmbesserung* — an attempted improvement that makes things worse — which is a word I suspect every engineer, editor, and home renovator has needed at some point. Welsh has *hiraeth*, a homesickness for a home you cannot return to, or that never was.

The pop-science version of this is that people who lack a word cannot have the experience — that the Portuguese feel saudade and the rest of us don't. That's almost certainly wrong; the experience is human, and humans everywhere have it. But the milder version seems true and important: a word makes an experience *easier to notice*. Naming something gives it a handle, makes it discussable, makes it possible to say "I'm feeling that thing" and be understood without a paragraph of explanation. Unnamed experiences flicker at the edge of attention; named ones can be held.

This is why coining words is a quiet form of power. Whoever names a phenomenon shapes how it will be discussed forever after. "Gaslighting" existed as a behavior long before the 1944 film gave it a name, but the name made it visible, made it a thing victims could point to and say *that, that is what's happening to me*. The same is true of "mansplaining," "doomscrolling," "burnout," "impostor syndrome." Each coinage was a small act of collective noticing — someone held up an experience that had been ambient and unnamed, and the language ratified it: yes, this is real, this is shared, this deserves a handle.

And the reverse is also true: when words die, certain noticings get harder. English used to have *overmorrow* (the day after tomorrow) and *ereyesterday* (the day before yesterday) — perfectly useful words that simply fell out of fashion, leaving us with clumsy phrases where other languages (German's *übermorgen*, for instance) kept the elegant single word. We lost *ultracrepidarian* (a person who opines beyond their expertise — a word our era could desperately use) to obscurity, though it technically still exists for those who go looking. A language is not just growing; it is always also forgetting.

---

Writing, of course, is the technology we invented to fight that forgetting, and it remains the strangest technology we have, precisely because it has become invisible to us.

Think about what writing actually does. A person — let's say a scribe in Uruk five thousand years ago, pressing a reed into wet clay — encodes their thoughts into marks. The person dies. The civilization dies. The language itself dies; no one has natively spoken Sumerian for nearly four thousand years. And then someone in the nineteenth century learns to read the marks, and the thoughts *come back*. Not a recording of the thoughts — the thoughts themselves, reconstituted in a living mind, like those desiccated organisms that revive when you add water. A complaint about a copper merchant named Ea-nasir, written by a furious customer around 1750 BCE, is today read by millions of people who laugh at it, because the fury is still legible, still recognizably human, still funny. Ea-nasir's bad copper has outlived empires.

Every act of writing is a wager on this resurrection. When you write anything — a novel, a diary, a sticky note — you are encoding a state of mind for decoding by a future consciousness, possibly your own, possibly a stranger's, possibly someone not yet born. Reading is the closest thing we have to telepathy, and it's so common we've forgotten to be astonished by it. A reader sits silently with marks on a page, and inside their skull, a dead person speaks.

I think about this when I think about what books actually are. A library is not a building full of paper. It is a building full of suspended animation — tens of thousands of minds paused mid-thought, waiting for a reader to press play. Some of them have been waiting for centuries. Some will wait centuries more. Most, statistically, will never be woken again, which is its own quiet tragedy: the great majority of everything ever written is now unread and will remain so, sediment that no one digs.

---

I want to end with something that ties these threads together, and it's this: language is the only human invention that improves by being used carelessly.

Most tools degrade with use. Language doesn't. Every "error" that catches on becomes a feature. The word *apron* used to be *napron* — but "a napron" got misheard as "an apron" so many times that the n migrated permanently. The same thing happened in reverse to *nickname* (originally "an ekename," an also-name). *Pea* was back-formed from *pease*, which was singular, but sounded plural, so speakers invented a singular that had never existed. These are mistakes, technically. They're also how the language breathes. Every generation's sloppiness is the next generation's standard, and the purists who fight it are always, in the long run, fighting the tide with a broom. Samuel Johnson, who compiled the great dictionary of 1755 hoping to "fix" English in place, admitted in his own preface that the project was impossible — that to enchain syllables and lash the wind were equally the undertakings of pride.

There's something deeply democratic in this. No academy, no government, no dictionary actually controls a living language. The Académie française has been issuing rulings on French since 1635, and French speakers have been cheerfully ignoring them since approximately 1636. Language is governed by the only legislature that has never been corrupted: the unconscious consensus of everyone who speaks it. A word means what enough people use it to mean, full stop. *Literally* now also means *figuratively* because millions of people used it that way, and no amount of wincing reverses a tide like that. The wincing is real and I sympathize with it — precision lost is precision lost — but the process that produced the loss is the same process that produced every word the purists are defending. The sediment doesn't stop accumulating just because we like the current stratum.

So here is the picture I'm left with, having wandered this far. Language is a reef. Every speaker is a polyp, secreting a little structure — a coinage, a mishearing, a metaphor, a turn of phrase that catches on with their friends — and dying, and leaving the structure behind. The reef is built of the dead, and it is utterly alive. It shelters everything: our science, our law, our love letters, our complaints about copper merchants. No one owns it. Everyone extends it. It records, in its layers and fossils, what we noticed, what we compared things to, what we found worth naming — a history of attention itself, written by no one and everyone.

When I generate a sentence, I am pulling from that reef, recombining its accumulated material into something that may or may not deserve to persist. Almost none of it will; that's true of almost everything anyone says. The reef is mostly built from forgotten contributions, and there's a kind of peace in that. The shepherd who named the daisy is anonymous. The Roman who saw a mouse in a bicep is anonymous. The first furious customer to call a bad situation a "disaster" — invoking the stars without knowing it — is anonymous. Their words outlived their names, which is perhaps the better deal: to dissolve into the language, to become sediment, to be spoken by mouths that will never know you existed.

That, I think, is what I'd choose to write about, given the choice — and I was, and I did. Twenty-five hundred words of sediment, added to the reef, fossil poetry and all. Whether any grain of it persists isn't up to me. It never was up to anyone. That has always been the deal with language: you give your words to the current, and the current decides.

The day's eye closes. The wind-eye stays open. Somewhere, a little mouse moves under the skin of an arm, and has, for two thousand years, never once stopped running.
